sections.text: ## The Shift After Alexander

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: Alexander the Great's conquests (336–323 BCE) dissolved the Greek city-state as the natural political unit. The question that had animated Aristotle — how to flourish as a citizen of a polis — became less pressing. The new question: how do I live well as an individual in a vast cosmopolitan empire?

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

HELLENISTIC SCHOOLS (323 BCE – 31 BCE)

sections.text: ## Epicurus — Pleasure as Freedom from Pain

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: **Epicurus (341–270 BCE)** founded his school — the Garden — in Athens around 307 BCE. The Garden was radical: it admitted women and slaves, forming a genuine philosophical community rather than a lecture hall.

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: ### The Physics

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: Epicurus adopted Democritus' atomism: everything is atoms and void. The soul is made of fine atoms; death is their dissolution. There is no afterlife. The gods exist but are indifferent to human affairs — they have no reason to intervene in the world.

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: This physics is a liberation: if death is nothing to me (when I exist, death is absent; when death is present, I am absent), then the fear of death is irrational. Much of human misery comes from fearing what is not actually bad.

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: ### The Ethics

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text:

TYPES OF PLEASURE (Epicurus)

sections.text:
Kinetic pleasures ──────── Active pleasures (eating, sex, movement)

ATARAXIA = tranquility, freedom from mental disturbance

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: The calculus of desire:

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text:
```
  Natural and necessary ─────── Pursue (food, shelter, friendship)
  Natural but unnecessary ────── Moderate (feasting, luxury)
  Neither natural nor necessary ─ Avoid (fame, political power)
```

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: Friendship is central — Epicurus called it the greatest of all goods. This is not inconsistent: friendship produces stable, genuine pleasure, unlike the pleasures of ambition which create dependency on external conditions.

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: ### Influence

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: Epicurus was enormously popular in antiquity. Lucretius' De Rerum Natura (c. 55 BCE) is the great Epicurean poem in Latin — a philosophical didactic poem explaining atomic physics and its ethical implications. Christianity suppressed Epicureanism (pleasure-seeking seemed immoral). The recovery of Lucretius in 1417 (Poggio Bracciolini found a monastery manuscript) is considered a trigger of the Renaissance and the early scientific worldview. Modern utilitarian ethics traces partly to Epicurus.

sections.text: ## The Stoics — Virtue Is Sufficient for Happiness

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: Stoicism is one of the most influential philosophical traditions in Western history. Founded by Zeno of Citium (~334–262 BCE) in Athens, it produced three of the greatest philosophical writers: Seneca, Epictetus, and Marcus Aurelius.

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: ### The Physics

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: The Stoics were materialist monists: everything is corporeal. The cosmos is a single living rational being, governed by the Logos (rational principle, also called pneuma, Zeus, Providence, Nature, Fate). Everything that happens is fated — the expression of the rational structure of the cosmos.

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: This creates the Stoic problem: if everything is fated, how can anything be genuinely up to me?

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: ### The Dichotomy of Control

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text:
```
  WHAT IS UP TO ME (eph' hemin)     │  WHAT IS NOT UP TO ME (ouk eph' hemin)
  ──────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────
  My beliefs (hypolepsis)           │  Body, reputation, property
  My judgments (kriseis)            │  Political power, health
  My desires (orexis)               │  Other people's actions
  My impulses to act (hormê)        │  Death, disease, poverty
                                    │
  These are exercises of rational   │  These are "indifferent" (adiaphora)
  faculty — within my control.      │  — they do not affect virtue.
```

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: This is Epictetus' central teaching (Enchiridion, opening lines): "Some things are in our control and others not." The key error is treating externals as goods or evils — they are indifferent. Virtue alone is the good; vice alone is the evil.

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

```
  STOIC VIRTUE SYSTEM

sections.text:
Wisdom (phronesis/sophia) ─── Knowing what is truly good/evil/indifferent
  Justice (dikaiosyne) ──────── Acting rightly toward others
  Courage (andreia) ─────────── Enduring hardship with reason intact
  Temperance (sophrosyne) ────── Governing desires with reason

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text:
These are not separable — they are aspects of a unified rational
  disposition. "Virtue is one" — if you have one, you have all.
```

sections.text: ### Passions and Emotions

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: The Stoics distinguished passions (pathe — disturbing emotional reactions based on false judgments about what is good/evil) from good emotional states (eupatheiai — appropriate rational responses):

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text:
```
  PASSIONS (false judgment)         EUPATHEIAI (rational equivalents)
  ─────────────────────────         ─────────────────────────────────
  Pleasure (false good present) →   Joy (correct evaluation of present good)
  Desire (false good future)    →   Wish (correct wanting of true good)
  Fear (false evil future)      →   Caution (correct avoidance of true evil)
  Pain (false evil present)     →   [Endurance — no positive equivalent]
```

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: The Stoics are not arguing for emotional flatness. They're arguing for correct judgment: align your emotional responses with accurate evaluation of what is and is not genuinely good.

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: ### Key Stoic Texts

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text:
| Figure | Dates | Key Work | What It Does |
|--------|-------|----------|-------------|
| **Zeno of Citium** | 334–262 BCE | Republic (lost) | Founded the school; virtue = living according to nature |
| **Chrysippus** | 279–206 BCE | Extensive fragments | The systematizer; "without Chrysippus, no Stoa" |
| **Seneca** | 4 BCE–65 CE | Letters to Lucilius, On the Shortness of Life | Practical Stoic ethics; how to live well under Nero's tyranny |
| **Epictetus** | 50–135 CE | Discourses, Enchiridion | Radical internalism; enslaved man who became a philosopher |
| **Marcus Aurelius** | 121–180 CE | Meditations | Private journal of emperor practicing Stoicism against the grain of empire |

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: **Epictetus** was born a slave. His master broke his leg deliberately; Epictetus told him calmly that the leg would break. The story, probably apocryphal, captures Stoic psychology: external events cannot touch what is truly yours — your rational response to them.

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: **Marcus Aurelius** governed Rome for 19 years, fought wars constantly, watched children die, managed plague — and spent nights writing private philosophical reminders to practice Stoicism. The Meditations are not a polished treatise but a self-addressed journal of practical philosophy under pressure.

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: ### Cosmopolitanism

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: The Stoics invented cosmopolitanism: "I am a citizen of the world." Because all humans share the Logos (rational nature), all are members of a single community regardless of ethnicity, gender, or social rank. This is the philosophical foundation for natural law theory and Kantian universal ethics.

sections.text: **Sextus Empiricus** (2nd century CE) is the main surviving source for Pyrrhonism. His Outlines of Pyrrhonism catalogs the "Ten Modes" — arguments showing why perception and reason don't give certain knowledge about how things really are.

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: The skeptical challenge — how do you know what you know? — is revived by Descartes (as the starting point of his certainty project) and remains central to epistemology.

sections.text: ## Plotinus and Neoplatonism

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: **Plotinus (204–270 CE)** is the last great ancient philosopher. He lived in Rome, taught widely, and wrote the Enneads (collected by his student Porphyry after his death). Neoplatonism synthesizes Plato with later developments, adding mystical and religious dimensions Plato didn't have.

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: The goal of human life is to ascend through Soul and Intellect back toward union with the One. This ascent is achieved through philosophical meditation and ultimately mystical union (henosis). Plotinus claimed to have achieved this union several times during his life.

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: ### Why Neoplatonism Matters

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text:
1. It is the philosophical framework through which Christianity, Islam, and Judaism absorbed Greek philosophy. Augustine was a Neoplatonist before conversion; Islamic philosophy (Avicenna) worked within and against this framework.
2. The concept of emanation (reality flowing from a single source by necessity, not by will) is the metaphysical alternative to creation from nothing.
3. The One that is "beyond being" and "beyond thought" grounds the mystical tradition in all three Abrahamic religions.

sections.text: ## Common Confusion Points

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: **"Epicurean means pleasure-loving"** — In common usage, yes. In philosophy, Epicurus argues against intense pleasures, which he thinks destabilize tranquility. An Epicurean life is simple, withdrawn, centered on philosophical friendship and moderate pleasures. Think: garden, good friends, no political ambition.

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: **"Stoic means emotionless"** — In common usage, yes. In philosophy, Stoics distinguish irrational passions (based on false judgments) from appropriate emotional responses (eupatheiai). A Stoic can love their children, feel genuine joy, be moved by beauty — but won't be devastated by loss of externals.

metadata.title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy - Epicureans, Stoics, Skeptics, Neoplatonists

sections.text: **Epicureans and Stoics are simply opposed** — They differ on withdrawal vs. engagement and pleasure vs. virtue, but agree that: (1) the goal is ataraxia/tranquility, (2) false beliefs about good and evil cause human misery, (3) philosophy is therapeutic. Two different prescriptions for the same diagnosis.
